questions.question: Aerosol-transmitted organisms that are not thought to spread person-to-person.

parts.text: Name 2 organisms that can be transmitted by aerosols, but are not thought to be transmitted person-to-person.

parts_raw.text: Name 2 organisms that can be transmitted by aerosols, but are not thought to be transmitted person-to-person.

questions.model_answer: (1) Coxiella burnetii (Q fever) - acquired by inhalation of contaminated aerosols; person-to-person spread is negligible, so hospitalized patients need not be isolated unless undergoing an aerosolizing procedure or recently delivered. (2) Coccidioides immitis (or, equally acceptable, Histoplasma capsulatum, Brucella spp., or Legionella pneumophila) - acquired by aerosol inhalation without person-to-person transmission.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only Coxiella is grounded in this chapter; Coccidioides/Histoplasma/Brucella/Legionella are established non-person-to-person aerosol pathogens from general Mandell/CDC knowledge.

questions.question: Expected serologies in chronic (persistent focalized) Coxiella burnetii infection.

parts.text: What would you expect serologies to be for a chronic coxiella infection?

parts_raw.text: What would you expect serologies to be for a chronic coxiella infection.

questions.model_answer: In chronic Q fever the phase I IgG titre is high and characteristically equals or exceeds the phase II titre (reverse of acute infection). A phase I IgG >=1:800 by immunofluorescence is a minor/added-major criterion for Q fever endocarditis, and a rising or persistently elevated phase I IgG (>1:800-1:1024 in the US/Netherlands, >1:6400 in France) indicates persistent focalized infection such as endocarditis, vascular infection, or osteomyelitis. A phase I complement-fixation titre >=1:200 has also been considered diagnostic of chronic Q fever.

cohort_answer.text: Redbook: Confirmation of persistent (chronic) Q fever is based on an increasing phase I IgG titer (typically ≥1:1024) that often is higher than the phase II IgG titer and an identifiable nidus of infection (eg, endocarditis, vascular infection, osteomyelitis, chronic hepatitis).

parts.text: What test would you order to diagnose and what values represent a positive test?
Three clinical manifestations of Q fever.
How would you treat this presentation?
Name of pathogen implicated in Q fever.

parts_raw.text: What test would you order to diagnose and what values represent a positive test?
How would you treat this presentation?
Name of pathogen implicated in Q-fever

questions.model_answer:
a) Order serology by indirect immunofluorescence (with PCR of blood/tissue as an adjunct, most useful early). This osteomyelitis/discitis represents persistent focalized (chronic) infection, so the diagnostic value is a high phase I IgG >=1:800 by immunofluorescence (phase I IgG equal to or higher than phase II); PET is particularly useful for detecting osteoarticular/vascular infection.
b) (1) Self-limited febrile illness (2) Pneumonia (3) Hepatitis (endocarditis/vascular infection and osteomyelitis are also accepted).
c) Doxycycline 100 mg PO BID plus hydroxychloroquine 200 mg PO TID for a prolonged course (approx 18 months), with monthly clinical/serologic monitoring and baseline plus 6-monthly ophthalmologic exams for hydroxychloroquine retinal toxicity.
d) Coxiella burnetii.

questions.model_answer:
a) Diagnose with indirect immunofluorescence serology (PCR of blood useful early, before seroconversion; biopsy/immunochemistry of tissue is definitive). In acute infection phase II antibodies predominate (phase II IgG > phase I) - the opposite of chronic disease. Confirmation is a fourfold rise between acute and convalescent sera (most seroconvert by 2-3 weeks) or, per CDC, a single phase II IgG >=1:128 as probable infection; a negative test in the first week does not exclude Q fever.
b) (1) Self-limited febrile illness (2) Pneumonia (3) Hepatitis (also endocarditis/vascular infection, osteomyelitis).
c) This osteomyelitis/discitis is persistent focalized infection: doxycycline 100 mg PO BID plus hydroxychloroquine 200 mg PO TID for a prolonged course (about 18 months), with clinical, serologic and ophthalmologic monitoring.
d) Coxiella burnetii.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Serology, PCR, biopsy. Acute infection: Phase 1 IgG (to diagnose osteomyelitis/endocarditis) would look lower than Phase 2 for acute infection - reverse true in chronic infection (rising phase 1 IgG titer higher than phase 2). Negative test in first week does not rule out Q fever. Phase 2 IgG: acute rise in acute/convalescent serology by 4-fold, or (per CDC) single positive IgG Phase 2 of >1:128; chronic >=1:800 (Major Duke Criteria). Syndromes: A self-limited flu-like illness; Pneumonia; Hepatitis. Treatment: Doxycycline plus hydroxychloroquine for 18 months. Pathogen: Coxiella burnetii
